At nap time in the crèche, the curtains were drawn and the room was dim. Deepak, five, sat up suddenly and pointed.
“Ganga-didi! A monster by the door!”
Ganga tiptoed over and switched on the small lamp. On the hook hung a long black raincoat with a hood.
“Look, it's Mr Das's raincoat,” she whispered. “Want to touch it?”
Deepak touched the sleeve. “It's just a coat.”
“Just a coat. Shall I leave the lamp on?”
He nodded, lay down and held her hand until his eyes closed.

qa.q: What was hanging on the hook?
qa.a: A long black raincoat with a hood.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when he saw the shape by the door?
qa.a: He felt frightened, thinking it was a monster.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that helped Deepak separate imagination from reality?
qa.a: She switched on the lamp and let him touch the coat so he could see and feel what it really was.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel when Deepak holds her hand and falls asleep?
qa.a: She likely feels tender and relieved that he feels safe again.

grounding: A crèche helper helps a five-year-old see that an imagined monster is only a coat, and comforts him.

I'm Nitin, Dilnaz's uncle. On Saturday I was babysitting, and at bedtime Dilnaz, five, screamed. “Chachu! There's a wolf on the wall!”
It was the shadow of the window grille and a plant, stretched by the street light.
I sat on her bed and made a shadow with my hands: a dog. Then a bird. Then a wolf.
“It's your hands!” she said.
“And the one on the wall?”
She looked. “It's the plant.” Then she made her own wobbly bird.
I don't know if she really believed me. But she fell asleep.

qa.q: What made the shadow on the wall?
qa.a: The window grille and a plant, stretched by the street light.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when she saw the wolf shadow?
qa.a: She felt scared, screaming for her uncle.

qa.q: How did the hand-shadow game help Dilnaz?
qa.a: It showed her how shadows are made, so she could see the wolf was only the plant.

qa.q: How does Nitin see his success?
qa.a: Nitin is unsure whether she fully believed him, but relieved that she fell asleep.

grounding: An uncle helps a five-year-old see that a scary shadow is not a real wolf.

For the planets test, most children tried to learn the order by reading the chapter again and again. Imran (ten) did something different.

qa.a: She likely feels proud and happy that her student's effort paid off.

Ganga Nani gave me a riddle at dinner. “A farmer has a goat, a tiger and a bundle of grass. His boat can carry him and one thing. If he leaves the goat with the grass, the goat eats it. If he leaves the tiger with the goat, the tiger eats the goat. How does he get them all across?”

In Class 6 our teacher asked us to write a paragraph: “Should school start later?” I'm Rafiq, and I thought it would be easy. I wrote, “Yes, because I'm sleepy.” That was it.
Ms Gurleen gave it back with a note: “Why? Give three reasons. Start with your opinion. End by saying it again.”

It was the first time a paragraph felt like a building instead of a pile of bricks.

qa.a: Ms Gurleen is likely pleased to see the advice used and the argument made clearly.

On Saturdays in Toronto, Hana, ten, went with her friend Esther to the market, and then home to her grandmother.
At the market stall she said to the seller, in English, “Two apples, please.” With Esther she giggled in a mix of English and the French they learned at school. “C'est trop cher!”
When she opened the door at home, she bowed a little and said, in Korean, “Halmeoni, I'm home.” Her grandmother smiled and answered in Korean.
Esther, following her in, whispered, “How do you know which one to use?”

Science note, Class 4. Teacher: Pema.
Today we did “sink or float.” Before each test, children wrote a guess.
Yusuf (nine) guessed the big wooden block would sink, “because it's heavy.” It floated. He stared at it. He guessed the small steel key would float, “because it's tiny.” It sank.
He said, “Wait. It's not about big or small.” He tried a plastic lid, then a coin, writing each result.
At the end he wrote: “My guesses were wrong but I learned something.”
Next step: we'll try the same objects in salty water next week.

Tarun and I planted two bean seeds last week. One in a cup on the window, one in a cup inside the cupboard. My guess: the cupboard one would grow slower because no sun.

In the hot afternoon in their village near Bikaner, Parul, eleven, and her friend Ankita had two ice cubes from the shop fridge.
“Which will melt first,” said Parul, “in the clay pot or the steel glass?”
Ankita guessed steel. “Steel gets hot.” Parul guessed the same.
They put one cube in each and sat in the shade, checking every few minutes.
The steel one melted first. But the clay pot's outside was wet and cool when Parul touched it.
“Why is the pot sweating?” Ankita asked.
Parul took out her notebook. “Let's write it down and ask Sir tomorrow.”

qa.q: Where did they put the ice cubes?
qa.a: One in the clay pot and one in the steel glass.

qa.q: How did the girls feel when the pot's outside was wet?
qa.a: They felt curious and puzzled, wanting to know why the pot was sweating.

qa.q: What did Parul do that shows good scientific thinking?
qa.a: She wrote down what happened and planned to ask the teacher instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might their teacher react to their question the next day?
qa.a: The teacher may be pleased and use it to explain how clay pots keep things cool.

grounding: Two village girls guess, test and observe how ice melts in clay and steel.
